cards.q: Describe the historical development of public international law. Name four turning points and explain for each how it changed who makes international law and for whom it is valid. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Modern international law begins with the Peace of Westphalia 1648 ('classical' international law of formally equal European sovereigns, 1648–1918); the October Revolution 1917, decolonisation after 1945 and the end of the East–West conflict in 1989 each changed the circle of states whose consent makes the law.
• Roots: binding agreements between powers are some 3,000 years old (Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty after the battle of Kadesh, 13th century BC); ideas — Bartolus (14th century: par in parem non habet imperium), Bodin 1576 (sovereignty), Grotius 1625 (De iure belli ac pacis: law between rulers without a superior legislator), Vattel 1758 (equality of states).
• 1648 Westphalia (Münster and Osnabrück): a settlement negotiated by a congress of formally equal states instead of being imposed by emperor or pope → horizontal order of sovereign states. Classical law (1648–1918) was the law of a small circle of European states and still allowed war as a lawful instrument; it produced multilateral conferences (Congress of Vienna 1815), the first IOs, humanitarian law (Solferino 1859 → Red Cross committee 1863, Geneva Convention 1864) and arbitration (Alabama claims 1872).
• 1917 October Revolution: a state challenged the system from outside (Soviet Russia rejected 'bourgeois' international law and repudiated the tsarist debts); after 1945 the East–West divide paralysed the Security Council through the veto.
• Decolonisation after 1945: from 51 founding UN members to 193; self-determination (GA Res 1514, 1960); the new majority demanded a say in rules it had not made → more states must consent, general practice becomes harder to establish.
• 1989 end of the East–West conflict: a '(seeming?) unity' — revival of the Security Council (Iraq–Kuwait 1990–91, ICTY 1993, ICTR 1994), Rome Statute of the ICC 1998; later renewed division (Kosovo 1999, Iraq 2003, Ukraine 2014/2022).
Memorise: roots (Kadesh, Grotius 1625) · 1648 Westphalia → classical IL 1648–1918 (Europe, war lawful) · 1917 challenge from outside · decolonisation 51 → 193 · 1989 (seeming?) unity

cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. 'Under the principle of sovereign equality all states must have the same influence. The veto of the five permanent members of the Security Council and weighted voting in the IMF therefore violate international law.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — sovereign equality means formal legal equality (equal status, rights and duties), not equal influence; states may, as an exercise of their sovereignty, consent by treaty to unequal voting arrangements such as the veto or IMF quotas.
• Content (Art 2(1) UN Charter; Friendly Relations Declaration 1970): states are juridically equal, have equal rights and duties and are equal members of the international community 'notwithstanding differences of an economic, social, political or other nature'; Vattel: a dwarf is as much a man as a giant. Consequences: immunity (par in parem), 'one state, one vote' as the default (Art 18(1) Charter), consent as the basis of obligations.
• Equality is a legal category, not a description of power: states are deeply unequal economically and politically.
• Departures are lawful because they were agreed: the same Charter that proclaims sovereign equality creates the permanent seats (Art 23) and the veto (Art 27(3)), and every member accepted it; IMF members accepted votes weighted by quota (the US, with about 16.5 %, can block decisions requiring 85 %). Without such agreement the default of equal votes applies.
Memorise: sovereign equality = formal (Art 2(1), FRD 1970, Vattel) ≠ equal power · default one state, one vote · veto / weighted votes lawful because consented by treaty

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: Minera SA, a company incorporated and with its registered office in State Nordal, obtained a mining concession from State Quivar. Clause 18 of the concession contract reads: 'The concessionaire waives any right to request the diplomatic protection of its home State in matters relating to this contract; all disputes shall be decided exclusively by the courts of Quivar.' Quivar later expropriates the mine without any compensation, and Quivar's Supreme Court dismisses Minera's action in a final judgment. Nordal wants to take up Minera's case against Quivar; Quivar invokes Clause 18. Assess. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Clause 18 does not bar Nordal — diplomatic protection is a right of the state, not of the company, so a private party cannot waive it (Calvo clause); at most the clause confirms the duty to exhaust local remedies, which Minera has done.
• Calvo doctrine (Carlos Calvo, 19th-century Argentine jurist): foreign investors are treated like nationals and may seek redress only before local courts; Calvo clauses contain the investor's waiver of home-state protection.
• Rule: in exercising diplomatic protection a state asserts its own right (Mavrommatis, PCIJ 1924; Arts 1–2 ILC Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection 2006) and is the sole judge whether to protect (Barcelona Traction 1970). An individual cannot dispose of a right that belongs to its state; the ILC notes that the clause, although regarded as regional custom by Latin American states, is hard to reconcile with international law if read as a complete waiver. North American Dredging (US–Mexico General Claims Commission 1926): the clause is valid only as an undertaking to use local remedies in contractual matters; it cannot deprive the government of its right to apply international remedies to violations of international law, such as a denial of justice — the claim failed there because the company had not tried the Mexican courts at all.
• Application: expropriation of a foreign-owned mine without compensation is an internationally wrongful act attributable to Quivar (Art 4 ARSIWA), not a mere contract dispute. The conditions are met: Nordal nationality (incorporation and registered office — Barcelona Traction; Art 9 DADP) and exhaustion of local remedies up to the Supreme Court (Art 14 DADP).
• Conclusion: Nordal may, at its discretion, espouse the claim. Note: if Minera and Quivar had consented to ICSID arbitration (e.g. via an investment treaty), Nordal could not exercise diplomatic protection in respect of that dispute unless Quivar failed to comply with the award (Art 27(1) ICSID Convention).
Memorise: Calvo clause = investor's waiver → ineffective against the STATE's right (Mavrommatis 1924; Art 2 DADP) · valid only as a local-remedies undertaking (North American Dredging 1926) · still: nationality + exhaustion + discretion · Art 27(1) ICSID

cards.q: The Austrian Land of Tyrol wants to conclude a binding agreement on a joint cross-border nature park with the Free State of Bavaria, a constituent state of Germany; nature protection falls within the autonomous competence of the Länder. (a) Can a constituent state of a federation conclude treaties under international law? (b) Under which conditions and in which procedure may Tyrol do so under Austrian constitutional law? (c) Could Tyrol conclude a similar agreement with France? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Only if and insofar as its federal constitution confers that capacity and the treaty partner accepts it — constituent states are at most partial, derived subjects; (b) yes, under Art 16 B-VG: a matter of the Land's autonomous competence, a neighbouring state or its constituent state as partner, federal government informed and consenting, conclusion by the Federal President; (c) no — France does not border Austria.
• (a) Every state possesses treaty-making capacity (Art 6 VCLT); the ILC draft provision on members of federal unions was deleted at the Vienna Conference 1969, so capacity depends on the federal constitution and the partner's acceptance. Constituent states are 'state-like subjects' with limited, derived personality (Bavaria: Art 32(3) German Basic Law — within Land legislative competence, with the consent of the federal government).
• (b) Art 16(1) B-VG: the Länder may conclude treaties with states bordering Austria or their constituent states in matters of their autonomous sphere of competence — Bavaria and nature protection qualify. Art 16(2): the Landeshauptmann must inform the federal government before negotiations start and obtain its consent before conclusion (deemed given unless refused within eight weeks of the request reaching the Federal Chancellery); the authorisation to negotiate and the conclusion are for the Federal President on the proposal of the Land government, countersigned by the Landeshauptmann. No Nationalrat approval: Art 50(1) Z 1 B-VG excludes treaties under Art 16(1).
• Federal control: the Land must terminate the treaty at the federal government's request, failing which the competence passes to the Federation (Art 16(3)); it must implement it, otherwise the Federation takes over, including legislation (Art 16(4)); the Federation supervises implementation (Art 16(5)).
• (c) France is not a neighbouring state → no Land treaty; only the Republic could conclude it (Federal President, Art 65(1) B-VG), with Bundesrat consent insofar as it regulates matters of the Länder's autonomous competence (Art 50(2) Z 2 B-VG), or Tyrol could agree a non-binding cooperation arrangement.
Memorise: federal units = treaty capacity only via federal constitution + partner's acceptance (ILC draft on federal units deleted 1969) · Art 16 B-VG: own competence + neighbour or its constituent state + federal consent (8 weeks) + Federal President · termination on federal request (16(3)) · no Nationalrat (50(1) Z 1)

cards.q: Classify international organizations according to (i) their membership, (ii) their field of activity and (iii) the scope of competences transferred to them, giving an example for each category. What distinguishes a supranational organization from an intergovernmental one, and from which two roots did international organizations historically develop? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: IOs are universal or regional, technical or political, and intergovernmental or supranational; the EU is supranational because its members transferred sovereign rights so that it legislates with direct effect for their citizens. Historically IOs grew from 19th-century administrative unions and from the peace organizations of the 20th century.
• (i) Membership: universal — open to all states (UN, WHO, UPU); regional — limited by geography (Council of Europe, EU, African Union, OAS).
• (ii) Field of activity: technical/functional — cross-border coordination (ITU, UPU, ICAO, WMO); political — maintenance of peace (League of Nations, UN); many are mixed.
• (iii) Competences: intergovernmental organizations organise cooperation; decisions usually need consensus or unanimity and must be implemented by the members (OECD, Council of Europe). Supranational: organs independent of the members (Commission, directly elected Parliament, Court of Justice with compulsory jurisdiction), majority decisions binding outvoted members, acts directly applicable or with direct effect and primacy over national law (Van Gend en Loos 1963, Costa v ENEL 1964).
• Roots: administrative unions solving technical coordination problems — river commissions (Rhine 1815, Danube 1856), International Telegraph Union 1865, Universal Postal Union 1874; peace organizations — League of Nations 1919, United Nations 1945. Permanent tension: every competence the IO gains is sovereignty given up by its members.
Memorise: universal / regional · technical / political · intergovernmental / supranational (EU: direct effect + primacy + majority) · roots: administrative unions (ITU 1865, UPU 1874) vs peace organizations (League 1919, UN 1945)

cards.topic: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases
cards.q: The specialized agency FUTURA, seated in State Domizilia, has set up a research institute without separate legal personality, rents a building for it and appoints Mr Explorator as its managing director. When the institute proves unprofitable, FUTURA halves his salary. To avoid bad publicity, FUTURA's Director-General expressly waives FUTURA's immunity for Explorator's action before the Domizilian labour court, which orders FUTURA to pay the arrears. FUTURA does not pay. Can Explorator have FUTURA's Domizilian bank account and the institute's laboratory equipment seized? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — the waiver covers only immunity from jurisdiction; FUTURA's property and assets remain immune from measures of execution unless FUTURA expressly waives that immunity as well, whatever the assets are used for.
• Sources: founding treaty, headquarters agreement and the Convention on the Privileges and Immunities of the Specialized Agencies 1947, if Domizilia is a party and applies it to FUTURA (for the UN itself: Art 105 Charter and the 1946 Convention, Sections 2–3). Section 4 (1947): agencies, their property and assets enjoy immunity from every form of legal process except where expressly waived in a particular case — 'no waiver of immunity shall extend to any measure of execution'. Section 5: premises inviolable; property and assets immune from search, requisition, confiscation, expropriation and any other form of interference by executive, administrative, judicial or legislative action.
• Application: the express waiver by the executive head made the action admissible and the judgment valid, but enforcement is a separate step requiring a second, express waiver. The institute is part of FUTURA, so its equipment is FUTURA's property. For states, too, consent to jurisdiction is not consent to execution (Art 20 UN Convention 2004), but without consent execution is possible against assets serving non-sovereign purposes when execution begins (Philippine Embassy, BVerfG 1977; Art 19 UN Convention 2004); IO immunity instead protects all assets — functional in rationale, absolute in practice.
• Consequence: Explorator depends on FUTURA paying voluntarily; FUTURA must comply in good faith and must provide appropriate modes of settlement (Section 31: internal appeal, an administrative tribunal such as the ILOAT if it has accepted its jurisdiction); Domizilia can raise the matter with FUTURA.
Memorise: IO: waiver of jurisdiction ≠ waiver of execution (Sect. 4 1947 / Sect. 2 1946) · assets immune from any interference, whatever their use (Sect. 5) · states: purpose of assets decides (Philippine Embassy; Arts 19–20 UNCSI) · Sect. 31 alternative settlement

cards.topic: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases
cards.q: Greenwatch, an environmental association registered under Austrian law with national sections in 40 countries, wants to make its voice heard when climate issues are discussed at the United Nations. (a) Can it obtain consultative status, from which organ and under which conditions? (b) Would it then be able to vote on ECOSOC resolutions or bring a case against a polluting state before the ICJ? (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) Yes — ECOSOC can grant consultative status under Art 71 UN Charter (details in ECOSOC Res 1996/31) on the recommendation of its Committee on NGOs; (b) no — the status gives access and a voice, not a vote, international legal personality or standing before the ICJ.
• (a) Art 71: ECOSOC may make suitable arrangements for consultation with NGOs concerned with matters within its competence. Conditions (Res 1996/31): activities relevant to ECOSOC's work and in line with the Charter, recognised standing or representative character, established headquarters with an executive officer, democratically adopted constitution, representative and accountable structure, not established by a governmental entity or by intergovernmental agreement, existence for at least two years. Categories: general, special, roster.
• (b) Rights: provisional agendas, attendance at public meetings as observers, written statements (general status up to 2,000 words, special status and roster 500), oral statements subject to the Council's approval; general-status NGOs may propose agenda items through the Committee on NGOs. No vote; contentious ICJ proceedings are open only to states (Art 34(1) ICJ Statute), and NGOs cannot request advisory opinions (Art 96 Charter). Influence is not personality — Greenwatch remains an NGO.
Memorise: Art 71 Charter + ECOSOC Res 1996/31 · Committee on NGOs recommends, ECOSOC decides · general / special / roster · access + written/oral statements, no vote · ICJ only for states (Art 34(1))

cards.topic: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases
cards.q: Distinguish the UN Human Rights Council from the Human Rights Committee. Describe the Council's legal basis, composition and working methods, and explain whether it can adopt decisions binding on a state. (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: The Human Rights Council is a political body of 47 states, a subsidiary organ of the General Assembly created in 2006, which reviews all UN members and adopts non-binding recommendations; the Human Rights Committee is the treaty body of 18 independent experts supervising the ICCPR.
• Council — basis: GA Res 60/251 of 15 March 2006 (Art 22 Charter), replacing the Commission on Human Rights (1946, an ECOSOC functional commission with 53 members at the end), whose credibility had collapsed because states with poor records used membership to shield themselves; seat Geneva.
• Composition: 47 states elected individually by secret ballot by an absolute majority of GA members, with equitable geographical distribution (Africa 13, Asia-Pacific 13, Eastern Europe 6, Latin America and Caribbean 8, Western Europe and others 7); three-year terms, no immediate re-election after two consecutive terms. Members must uphold the highest standards and undergo review; the GA may suspend a member committing gross and systematic violations by two thirds of members present and voting (Libya 2011, Russia 2022).
• Working methods: Universal Periodic Review of every UN member (peer review roughly every four to five years), special procedures (special rapporteurs, working groups), a confidential complaint procedure for consistent patterns of gross violations, commissions of inquiry, resolutions.
• Legal effect: recommendations only — the Council cannot bind states; binding measures remain reserved to the Security Council (Art 25, Chapter VII).
• Committee: organ of the ICCPR (Art 28), 18 independent experts, state reports (Art 40), general comments, individual communications under the First Optional Protocol; its 'views' are not formally binding but must be considered in good faith.
Memorise: Council = 47 states, GA Res 60/251 (2006), replaced Commission (53), UPR, suspension by 2/3 GA, recommendations only · Committee = 18 experts, Art 28 ICCPR, reports + OP1 communications, 'views'

cards.topic: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases
cards.q: Vienna is one of the four seats of the United Nations. Name four international organizations with their seat in Vienna and their main tasks. Why does the CTBTO still exist only as a 'Preparatory Commission', and is OPEC an international organization although it pursues the commercial interests of its members? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: E.g. the IAEA, UNIDO, the CTBTO Preparatory Commission and OPEC (plus the OSCE, whose IO status is disputed; UNODC is an office of the UN Secretariat, not a separate organization); the CTBTO is only preparatory because the Comprehensive Nuclear-Test-Ban Treaty 1996 has not entered into force, and OPEC is an IO because it was founded by states under international law with its own organs — a public-interest purpose is not part of the definition.
• IAEA (1957, Vienna from the start; a 'related organization', not a specialized agency): peaceful use of nuclear energy and safeguards verifying the Non-Proliferation Treaty (in force 1970). UNIDO (1966, Vienna since 1967, specialized agency since 1985): industrial development and poverty reduction. UNODC (UN Secretariat): drugs, crime and terrorism prevention. OSCE (successor of the CSCE, in Vienna since 1995): East–West security cooperation — its IO status is disputed for lack of a founding treaty.
• CTBTO: under Art XIV CTBT the treaty enters into force only after ratification by all 44 states listed in its Annex 2 (states with nuclear power or research reactors at the time); several of them (e.g. the USA, China, India, Pakistan, North Korea) have not ratified, and Russia withdrew its ratification in 2023, so only the Preparatory Commission (Vienna since 1997) builds up the global monitoring system (seismic, hydroacoustic, infrasound and radionuclide stations).
• OPEC (founded in Baghdad 1960, Vienna since 1965): member states, own organs (Conference, Secretariat), headquarters agreement with Austria; it sets production quotas — in substance an oil cartel. The definition of an IO (ARIO Art 2(a): instrument governed by international law + own international legal personality) looks at form and personality, not at the purpose.
Memorise: Vienna: IAEA, UNIDO, CTBTO PrepCom, OPEC (+ OSCE disputed, UNODC = UN Secretariat) · CTBT not in force (Art XIV: all 44 Annex 2 states) · OPEC = IO despite cartel purpose

cards.topic: Prohibition of the Use of Force and Non-Intervention
cards.q: Distinguish ius ad bellum from ius in bello. Describe how the prohibition of the use of force developed from the 19th century to the UN Charter, and explain what the Charter added compared with the Briand-Kellogg Pact. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Ius ad bellum governs WHETHER a state may resort to force, ius in bello (humanitarian law) HOW force must be used once a conflict exists; the law developed from an unlimited freedom to wage war, via the League's procedural limits (1919) and the renunciation of war (1928), to the Charter's comprehensive ban on the threat or use of force with only two exceptions.
• Distinction: ius ad bellum — Art 2(4), Art 51 and Chapter VII of the Charter; ius in bello — Hague Conventions 1899/1907, Geneva Conventions 1949 and Additional Protocols 1977. The two are independent: humanitarian law binds aggressor and defender alike, and lawful self-defence does not permit violations of humanitarian law.
• Until 1919: war was part of a state's external sovereignty — no ius ad bellum limit; only the 'humanisation' of war progressed (Geneva Convention 1864, Hague Conventions). The Drago-Porter Convention 1907 merely restricted force for the recovery of contract debts.
• League Covenant 1919: relative prohibition — disputes had to be submitted to arbitration, judicial settlement or the Council, and war was barred until three months after the award or report (Art 12, 'cooling-off'); afterwards war could remain lawful.
• Briand-Kellogg Pact 1928: the parties condemned recourse to war and renounced it as an instrument of national policy — but only 'war' was covered, there was no enforcement mechanism, and self-defence reservations were made; it later underpinned 'crimes against peace' at Nuremberg.
• UN Charter 1945: Art 2(4) prohibits any threat or use of force in international relations, not only war; the only exceptions are self-defence (Art 51) and Security Council measures under Chapter VII (Arts 39–42), which also supply the enforcement the Pact lacked; the prohibition is also customary law (Nicaragua 1986) and widely regarded as ius cogens.
Memorise: ad bellum = whether / in bello = how (independent) · before 1919 war lawful · League 1919 = procedure + 3-month cooling-off · Kellogg 1928 = war renounced, no enforcement · Charter 1945 = threat + use of force, 2 exceptions + Chapter VII

cards.q: Explain how human rights became a matter of international law rather than a purely domestic affair. Name the most important universal and regional human rights instruments and indicate their legal nature. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Until the 20th century a state's treatment of its own nationals was a domestic matter (only aliens were protected, through diplomatic protection); after early breaches (abolition of slavery, minority treaties after 1919) the UN Charter 1945 made human rights an international concern, followed by the UDHR 1948, the two Covenants 1966, specialised conventions and regional systems.
• Before 1945: human rights grew in domestic law (England, USA, France); internationally there were only the minimum standard for aliens, the fight against the slave trade and slavery (Slavery Convention 1926), humanitarian law, ILO labour standards (1919) and the minority treaties after World War I under League guarantee (e.g. the Treaty of St Germain 1919 for Austria; Minority Schools in Albania, PCIJ 1935).
• After 1945: Arts 1(3), 55(c) and 56 Charter — respect for human rights is a UN purpose and members pledge to cooperate; UDHR 1948 (GA Res 217 A (III)) — not binding per se, but partly custom or an authoritative interpretation of the Charter; ICCPR and ICESCR 1966 (in force 1976) — with the UDHR the 'International Bill of Rights'.
• Specialised UN treaties: Genocide Convention 1948, CERD 1965, CEDAW 1979, Convention against Torture 1984, Convention on the Rights of the Child 1989, Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities 2006 — binding treaties, most with a monitoring committee.
• Regional: ECHR 1950 (European Court of Human Rights, Strasbourg), American Convention 1969 (Inter-American Court, San José), African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights 1981 (African Court, Arusha); Council of Europe also: European Social Charter 1961, Charter for Regional or Minority Languages 1992, Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities 1995, Istanbul Convention 2011.
• Legal nature: treaties bind only their parties; core rights (prohibitions of genocide, torture, slavery, racial discrimination) are customary, owed erga omnes (Barcelona Traction 1970, para 34) and partly ius cogens. The individual is the holder of the rights, regardless of nationality — unlike diplomatic protection.
Memorise: domestic affair → minority treaties 1919 → Charter Arts 1(3), 55(c), 56 → UDHR 1948 (soft law / custom) → Covenants 1966 → CERD, CEDAW, CAT, CRC, CRPD → ECHR 1950, ACHR 1969, African Charter 1981 · core = custom, erga omnes, partly ius cogens

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: State Pavonia adopts a new nationality law: (1) every child of a Pavonian parent acquires Pavonian nationality, wherever born; (2) every child born on Pavonian territory acquires it; (3) a Pavonian who voluntarily acquires a foreign nationality loses Pavonian nationality; (4) a foreign woman who marries a Pavonian man automatically acquires Pavonian nationality, without any application. Neighbouring Rhodia argues that nationality is governed by international law and that Pavonia's law is unlawful. Assess each rule. (4 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: Rules (1)–(3) are lawful — each state determines who its nationals are, and descent, birth on the territory and loss on voluntary acquisition of another nationality are recognised connecting factors; rule (4) is inconsistent with international law (Art 9(1) CEDAW) and need not be recognised by other states.
• Principle: nationality is in principle within the reserved domain of states (Nationality Decrees in Tunis and Morocco, PCIJ 1923); Art 1 Hague Convention 1930: each state determines under its own law who are its nationals, but other states recognise that law only insofar as it is consistent with international conventions, custom and the principles of law generally recognised with regard to nationality. Nationality is the legal bond carrying rights (residence, return, political participation) and duties (taxes, military service).
• (1) Ius sanguinis (descent, e.g. Austria) and (2) ius soli (birth on the territory, e.g. the USA) are the classic modes of acquisition (Art 4 ILC Draft Articles on Diplomatic Protection: birth, descent, naturalisation, state succession); most states combine them. Rhodia cannot object. Limit on (2): children of foreign diplomats do not acquire the nationality solely by operation of the receiving state's law (Art II Optional Protocol to the VCDR concerning Acquisition of Nationality 1961, for its parties).
• (3) Loss on voluntary acquisition of a foreign nationality (cf. § 27 Austrian Nationality Act) and expatriation are lawful and cause no statelessness; deprivation must not be arbitrary (Art 15(2) UDHR) or discriminatory, and statelessness should be avoided (1961 Convention on the Reduction of Statelessness).
• (4) Automatic acquisition by marriage imposes a nationality without consent and applies only to women: Art 9(1) CEDAW (see also the Convention on the Nationality of Married Women 1957) requires that marriage to an alien neither automatically changes the wife's nationality nor forces the husband's nationality upon her. The ILC gives exactly this case as nationality acquired involuntarily 'in a manner inconsistent with international law' (commentary to Art 4 DADP): other states need not recognise it, and her former state of nationality may in principle still protect her.
• On the international plane a nationality lacking any genuine connection may also be non-opposable to another state (Nottebohm 1955, which the ILC reads narrowly).
Memorise: nationality = reserved domain (Tunis–Morocco 1923) but recognised only if consistent with IL (Hague 1930 Art 1) · ius sanguinis / ius soli / naturalisation / succession (Art 4 DADP) · diplomats' children excluded · loss on voluntary foreign nationality ok · no arbitrary deprivation (Art 15(2) UDHR) · forced nationality by marriage ✗ (Art 9(1) CEDAW)

cards.topic: States, Diplomatic Protection, Succession and Immunity
cards.q: In State Ruvia the army overthrows the elected president in a coup. The junta controls the capital and almost the entire territory; the president flees abroad and proclaims a government in exile. (a) Does the coup affect Ruvia's statehood and its treaties? (b) Are other states obliged to recognise the junta as Ruvia's government, and by which criteria do they decide? (c) Who represents Ruvia at the United Nations? (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: (a) No — a change of government, even an unconstitutional one, leaves the state's identity, treaties and obligations untouched; (b) there is no duty to recognise a government: the traditional test is effective control, some states add legitimacy, and many recognise only states; (c) the General Assembly decides through the credentials procedure, which may leave the previous representatives in place.
• (a) Continuity: the state is the subject of international law, the government merely its organ; Ruvia's treaties remain in force (Art 26 VCLT) and Ruvia is responsible for the junta's conduct (Art 4 ARSIWA). Even a temporary loss of effective government does not end statehood.
• (b) Recognition of a government is a discretionary unilateral act (express, or implied, e.g. by accrediting ambassadors). Effectiveness: Tinoco arbitration (1923) — a regime in effective control is the government regardless of its non-recognition by some states. Legitimacy: Tobar doctrine (1907) — no recognition of governments that seized power by revolution until they are constitutionally legitimised. Estrada doctrine (1930, Mexico): no statements on recognition at all, only maintaining or withdrawing diplomatic relations; the UK (since 1980) and many other states recognise states, not governments. States may keep treating the ousted elected president as the government (practice: Haiti 1991–94, Sierra Leone 1997), but without effective control his capacity to act for Ruvia (e.g. to invite foreign troops) is doubtful.
• (c) The GA's Credentials Committee examines credentials and the Assembly decides; in 2021 the Assembly deferred decisions on Afghanistan (Taliban) and Myanmar (junta), so the representatives of the previous governments kept the seats.
Memorise: coup ≠ new state (continuity, Art 26 VCLT, Art 4 ARSIWA) · no duty to recognise governments · effectiveness (Tinoco 1923) vs legitimacy (Tobar 1907) vs Estrada 1930 · UN seat = credentials (Afghanistan, Myanmar 2021)

cards.topic: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. 'The Security Council may only react to a concrete conflict by taking measures against the state responsible; it has no power to impose general and abstract obligations on all states, such as a duty to criminalise the financing of terrorism.' (2 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No, at least as a description of practice — acting under Chapter VII the Council has imposed general, abstract obligations on all states ('quasi-legislation'), e.g. Res 1373 (2001) and Res 1540 (2004); this is widely accepted but criticised as lacking legitimacy.
• Examples: Res 1373 (2001), after 9/11 — 'decides that all States shall' criminalise the financing of terrorism and freeze terrorist funds (Counter-Terrorism Committee); Res 1540 (2004) — all states must adopt effective laws preventing non-state actors from acquiring weapons of mass destruction; Res 2178 (2014) on foreign terrorist fighters.
• Legal basis: a general phenomenon (international terrorism, proliferation) can be a 'threat to the peace' (Art 39); the list in Art 41 is illustrative; decisions bind all members (Art 25) and prevail over conflicting treaty obligations (Art 103); the Council acts on behalf of all members (Art 24(1)).
• Limits and criticism: 15 members legislate for 193 without their consent; the Council must act in accordance with the purposes and principles (Art 24(2)) and is not legibus solutus; implementation must respect human rights (cf. Kadi, CJEU 2008).
Memorise: SC 'legislation': Res 1373 (2001) terrorism financing, Res 1540 (2004) WMD · Arts 39, 41 (open list), 25, 103 · criticised (legitimacy), bound by Art 24(2)

cards.topic: International Organizations II — the UN, and exam cases
cards.q: Do you agree with the following statement? Give reasons. 'The UN Charter is a treaty like any other: it binds only its parties, can only be amended with the consent of every party and has no special rank.' (3 points)
cards.a:
Short answer: No — formally the Charter is a multilateral treaty and the constituent instrument of an IO (Art 5 VCLT), but it has constitutional features: fundamental principles, organs with powers, enforcement, priority over other treaties (Art 103), effects on non-members (Art 2(6)) and amendment by majority (Art 108).
• Values: purposes and principles (Arts 1, 2) — sovereign equality, good faith, peaceful settlement, prohibition of force, most of them also customary law.
• Institutions and enforcement: six principal organs with distinct powers (Art 7); binding Council decisions (Art 25); collective security under Chapter VII (Arts 39–42).
• Hierarchy: Art 103 — obligations under the Charter prevail over obligations under any other international agreement (Lockerbie, provisional measures 1992).
• Non-members: Art 2(6) — the UN shall ensure that non-members act in accordance with the principles so far as necessary for international peace and security; with 193 members the Charter is quasi-universal.
• Amendment: Art 108 — amendments enter into force for ALL members once adopted by two thirds of the General Assembly and ratified by two thirds of the members including all five permanent members; outvoted members are bound, unlike under Art 40(4) VCLT.
• Interpretation: dynamic and functional — implied powers (Reparation 1949, Certain Expenses 1962).
Memorise: Charter = treaty + constitution: values (Arts 1, 2) · organs (Art 7) · enforcement (Ch VII) · Art 103 priority · Art 2(6) non-members · Art 108 majority amendment binds all
